entries.title: How a Ugandan lost 20 years of her life to xenophobia
entries.summary: After decades of building lives in South Africa, renewed anti-immigrant tensions in 2026 forced hundreds of African migrants to leave. A Ugandan who spent two decades in South Africa shared with DW how she's coping.
entries.content:
Uganda

How a Ugandan lost 20 years of her life to xenophobia

July 29, 2026

After decades of building lives in South Africa, renewed anti-immigrant tensions in 2026 forced hundreds of African migrants to leave. A Ugandan who spent two decades in South Africa shared with DW how she's coping.

When Winniefred Kabiri boarded a flight from Johannesburg to Kampala, she was leaving behind much more than a country. The Ugandan entrepreneur spent 20 years legally living in South Africa. During that time, she earned two university degrees and a postgraduate qualification, raised her children and established several businesses. "Initially everything was very successful. I created a life for myself and educated my children," Kabiri told DW.

But as anti-foreigner campaigns intensified in parts of South Africa this year, she no longer felt safe. "There was always a threat," she said. "But this year they gave ultimatums."

Kabiri is among more than 1,100 Ugandans evacuated from South Africa by their government following months of escalating xenophobic tensions, protests and intimidation targeting mostly African migrants. Uganda completed the first phase of its repatriation exercise in July, bringing home 1,102 nationals through six evacuation flights from Johannesburg.

South Africa has experienced recurring outbreaks of xenophobic violencesince the late 1990s, with migrants often blamed for unemployment, crimeand poor public services. Analysts say persistent inequality and economic frustration have continued to fuel anti-immigrant sentiment despite evidence that migrants contribute significantly to local economies. This year, however, many migrants say the atmosphere became markedly different.

Groups demanding tougher action against migrants organized public demonstrations and campaigns, while reports of intimidation, evictions and sporadic violence heightened fears among foreign communities. Many immigrants interviewed by DW said they felt vulnerableregardless of whether they possessed legal documentation.

Leaving behind years of investment in South Africa

For many returnees, like Kabiri, departure meant abandoning years of investment. She left businesses in commodities trading, mining, real estate and perfume manufacturing. She also left behind a professional network built over two decades. "Obviously,when you are told to leave and you're unprepared, you leave things behind," she said.

Another Ugandan returnee, Mathias Baguma, said he lost a business he spent years developing in Johannesburg. Baguma moved to South Africa in 2017 and later invested in a guesthouse, restaurant and retail operation. During the unrest, he says the property was attacked and looted.

"My business was vandalized. The shop was robbed, the restaurant broken into," he told DW. "I had to run for my life." Like many migrants across the continent, Baguma had viewed South Africa as a place where hard work could provide opportunities unavailable at home. Instead, he returned to Uganda with little more than personal belongings and memories of the life he had built.

Starting a new life in Uganda after fleeing xenophobia

Back in Uganda, the challenge for returnees is no longer escape, but rebuilding. Authorities say returning migrants were received at Entebbe airport and taken through orientation and reintegration programs, including counseling, health assessments and information sessions on government support initiatives.

Officials also introduced returnees to programs in agriculture, tourism, technology and small-business development aimed at helping themrestart their lives.

DW correspondent Frank Yiga said the Ugandan government moved quickly to organize transport, reception centers and psychosocial support for those affected. "The government helped prepare them for reintegration and informed them of the opportunities available," Yiga said.

Kabiri praised the initial response but acknowledged that rebuilding after 20 years abroad would be difficult. "I have to rebuild myself. I need to rebuild a new home and a business," she said.

She says family members have offered emotional support, but the financial reality remains daunting. For now, her focus is on creating a new future in Uganda. "East or West, home is best," she concluded.

 

This article was adapted from an AfricaLink Podcast. You can listen to the podcast here

Edited by: Chrispin Mwakideu.

entries.title: Iran signals gas price hike as fuel crisis looms
entries.summary: Iranian authorities want to dampen fuel consumption, but a sudden increase in gasoline prices risks social unrest as many Iranian households are already under severe economic pressure.
entries.content:
July 29, 2026

Iranian authorities want to dampen fuel consumption, but a sudden increase in gasoline prices risks social unrest as many Iranian households are already under severe economic pressure.

Iran is moving closer to politically sensitive changes in gasoline pricing as the government struggles with a widening gap between domestic fuel production and consumption, exacerbated by the ongoing conflict with the US.

On July 25, government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani said changes to fuel prices or rationing are "certain and unavoidable," although officials have yet to confirm whether the response will come through new quotas, higher prices or both.

Iran uses a tiered subsidized fuel price system with monthly quotas currently ranging from 1,500 tomans ($0.008) per liter at the lowest rung, to 5,000 tomans ($0.026) at the top. Iranian media have reported the new top rung for gasoline could jump to 10,000 tomans ($0.053) per liter, which would be nearly a 100% increase. The figure has not yet been officially confirmed.

Compared to the rest of the world, gasoline in Iran seems very inexpensive. But after years of sanctions and economic malaise, Iranians are also earning a lot less. Fuel may look exceptionally cheap in dollar terms, but so are the incomes used to pay for it.

For example, the basic monthly minimum wage in 2026 was set at around 16.6 million tomans, or about $87. Any hike in gas prices comes down hard on households.

The last major sudden increase in fuel prices in November 2019 triggered nationwide protests and one of the bloodiest crackdowns in the history of the Islamic Republic.

This time, the government faces another complication. Iran was already consuming more gasoline than it produced before the US launched the war in February. Damage to fuel infrastructure and restrictions on imports have made that imbalance harder and more expensive to manage.

Everyone needs fuel

Iranian officials argue that they need to suppress demand for gasoline with higher rates. But critics say that gasoline is a necessity and higher costs will not dampen demand.

A resident of Karaj, a small city near Tehran, said that said higher gasoline prices would quickly work their way through the economy, making everything more expensive.

"It will cause a chain reaction in the prices of goods and services, and the greatest pressure will ultimately fall on middle and lower-income households," he told DW anonymously for safety reasons.

A car that consumes 12 liters per 100 kilometers (19 miles per gallon) will not suddenly become more efficient because gasoline costs more, he said. Without better vehicles or effective public transport, motorists have few alternatives.

"Transport fares will go up when fuel becomes more expensive," he added.

Umud Shokri, an energy strategist and senior visiting fellow at George Mason University in the US, told DW that pricing could still play a role in reducing fuel consumption, but only as part of a much wider policy.

"Higher prices could discourage unnecessary driving and make fuel smuggling less profitable, but they would not solve the crisis by themselves," Shokri said.

A gradual increase for consumption above monthly quotas could help control demand, he said. But it would need to be combined with financial support for poorer households and substantial improvements in public transport.

Otherwise, he warned, higher prices could add to inflation and provoke social unrest.

How is oil powerhouse Iran short of gasoline?

Iran has some of the world's largest oil reserves, but crude oil production and gasoline production are two different things.

Shokri estimates that Iran currently produces around 121 million liters of gasoline per day, including blended fuel, while daily consumption is about 129 million liters. During holidays and peak travel periods, demand can rise even further.

The deficit has been developing for years.

Since 2019, domestic consumption has risen faster than production. Estimates cited in Iranian discussions suggest daily gasoline use has increased by around 39 million liters since 2019, while production capacity has risen by only around 16 million liters.

A country that once had surplus gasoline available for export has consequently become increasingly dependent on imports.

Shokri believes one of the quickest alternatives could be greater use of compressed natural gas, or CNG. Iran already has an extensive CNG network, but much of its capacity remains unused. Converting more vehicles to dual-fuel systems could reduce gasoline consumption relatively quickly.

Stronger rationing, measures against fuel smuggling and tougher efficiency standards could also help, he added.

Over the longer term, Iran would need to replace inefficient vehicles, improve public transport, electrify motorcycles and taxis, modernize refineries and increase strategic fuel storage, he said.

Imports could normally help compensate for shortages, but sanctions complicate payments, shipping and insurance. The war has added another layer of risk around maritime routes.

Russia might appear to be an obvious alternative supplier because of its close political relationship with Tehran. But Moscow has its own gasoline problem, with Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, pipelines and fuel storage sites disrupting production and contributing to shortages.

"Russia may be politically willing to help Iran, but currently it has less fuel available to export," Shokri said.

Iran's fuel problems predate US war

The war with the US has damaged fuel depots, storage tanks and parts of the distribution network, particularly around Tehran and Alborz. Shipping disruption also made imports more difficult and expensive.

However, Shokri cautions against overstating the physical destruction of Iran's fuel infrastructure.

He said there is currently no reliable evidence that Iran has permanently lost a large share of its gasoline production capacity. Refineries appear to have returned close to full operation.

"The war did not create Iran's gasoline crisis, but it made an already serious shortage more difficult and expensive to manage," he said.

It is unclear how the Iranian public will respond to another sharp fuel shock. The war has added another layer of anger, insecurity and frustration to grievances that were already building over living costs and declining purchasing power.

In that environment, a fuel price increase would not take place in an economic vacuum. It could become a trigger for wider discontent, making the government's decision over gasoline as much a political calculation as an economic one.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Lebanon's pilot zone plan: Can it work?
entries.summary: The Israeli army has handed so-called "pilot zones" back to the Lebanese, The move is meant to facilitate an end to fighting between Hezbollah and Israel, and to Israeli occupation. But locals and experts are skeptical.
entries.content:
Lebanon

Lebanon's pilot zone plan: Can it work?

July 29, 2026

The Israeli army has handed so-called "pilot zones" back to the Lebanese, The move is meant to facilitate an end to fighting between Hezbollah and Israel, and to Israeli occupation. But locals and experts are skeptical.

It has been just over a week since the so-called "pilot zone" plan was launched in Lebanon and the gap between the plan's ambitions and the reality on the ground remains stark.

According to the June 26 agreement between Lebanon, the US and Israel, the pilot zone plan is meant to see the Israeli military gradually redeploying out of parts of southern Lebanon it currently controls, which then allows the Lebanese army, or LAF, to move in.

After the armed wing of Lebanon's Hezbollah group fired rockets at Israel in March this year, Israel invaded Lebanon and now occupies a large swathe of the country’s south. The pilot zones are meant to end that. Once the LAF controls the zone, then Hezbollah can supposedly no longer operate from there. And once one zone has been secured, then the next will be actioned.

However there have been a number of troubling incidents already. The Israeli army shot at the vicinity of Lebanese soldiers as they approached one area last week and Israeli demolitions of homes and buildings in Lebanon continue, as do attacks with drones and bombs elsewhere in southern Lebanon.

The Israeli army's behavior jeopardizes the agreement from which the pilot zone plan originates, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun told the UN's human rights chief Volker Türk this week, when the latter visited Lebanon.

Pilot zone residents not impressed

Locals that DW spoke to, who live in the pilot zones, were also skeptical.

Hussein Kamaleddine, the mayor of Srifa, told DW he didn't understand why his village or the village of Froun had been made a pilot zone because Israeli soldiers had never even been stationed there.

"This is something that was forced upon us," Kamaleddine said. "It still doesn't make sense to us why these villages were considered pilot zones."

Other commentators have pointed out that lack of Israeli presence may be exactly why these towns were chosen as the first pilot zones: They don't directly impact northern Israel's security and it's a kind of soft launch for the plan.

Kamaleddine said he was happy to be back home in Srifa even though, he noted, he was surrounded by rubble. But he credited that homecoming to his community's resilience, not state support.

"Being back in Srifa now feels like a dream," he said. "But it's not thanks to the government. These so-called pilot zones are nothing but a scheme by the US and Israel."

Authorities from the village of Froun sent DW a written statement, expressing similar opinions. The town supported the LAF and that soldiers coming there had "preserved security and stability," they said.

But at the same time, they also completely rejected the pilot zone plan and described it "as serving the enemy [Israel] by prolonging its presence on Lebanese territory and creating a rift between the army and the people."

One of the major concerns about the pilot zone plan is that the LAF will be forced to confront Hezbollah fighters eventually, which could cause unrest, or even civil war. Hezbollah is thought to be as strong, or even stronger than, the Lebanese army.

Villages destroyed by Israeli army

Locals from another pilot zone village Zawtar al-Gharbieh (or West Zawtar) have been trying to get back home for several days now, mayor Abed Ezzeddine told DW.

And Israeli soldiers had definitely been there, Ezzeddine said. Almost all of the villagehas been destroyed.

"After seeing it, I can't describe it any other way: It's catastrophe upon catastrophe," Ezzeddine continued. "In principle, we cannot allow everyone to return at once, we're letting people in gradually. The plan is that once the army finishes clearing all the roads, God willing, everyone will be able to return."

The mayor has told other media this week that, despite being a pilot zone, the village doesn't feel safe. Another nearby village, Zawtar al-Sharqiyah (or East Zawtar) is still occupied by Israeli soldiers and the road going into his town runs through there, which makes it difficult to move around. When journalists from the Associated Press visited Zawtar al-Gharbieh this week, they heard explosions nearby and saw Israeli drones overhead.

How to tell if pilot zones work

Beyond the current problems on the ground, there are also major theoretical issues with the pilot zone plan.

"The framework Lebanon signed does not specify a withdrawal timetable and there is still no clarity on how disarming Hezbollah is defined, what the success criteria for disarmament are, and which party is responsible for determining whether these benchmarks are being met," explains Randa Slim, lead for the Middle East program at the US-based Stimson Center.

"Until the pilot zones include areas inside Israel's 'yellow line' and we see tangible evidence of Israeli forces withdrawing gradually from these areas, they serve, in my opinion, as Israeli smokescreens for an indefinite occupation in southern Lebanon," Slim argued.

This week Israeli prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu seemed to confirm that, saying Israel would not be withdrawing soldiers from Lebanon anytime soon.

"I'm not sure many people have much confidence that the agreement is a pathway to a constructive endgame here, whether in terms of facilitating the disarmament of Hezbollah or advancing an Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon," Julien Barnes-Dacey, director of the Middle East program at the European Council on Foreign Relations, or ECFR, told DW. "The terms have been shaped by Israel and give Netanyahu the space to … facilitate the country’s ongoing occupation of southern Lebanon."

Positives about pilot zones?

It's a bad deal but now that Lebanon has signed it, it must make the pilot zones work, Michael Young, a senior editor at the Carnegie Middle East Center in Beirut, argued in a July 21 commentary for UAE-based media outlet The National.

The Lebanese government must insist locals be allowed to return to their homes. Without it, the scheme is useless, Young wrote. And if the LAF does manage to control the pilot zones they move into, "this could serve as leverage to compel the Israelis to widen the areas of Lebanese control, since it is unlikely Hezbollah would seek a confrontation with the Lebanese army," Young concluded.

Also still being debated is which neutral party could monitor whether the pilot zones have been successful. In late June, France and Italy said they would be willing to lead an "international coalition to support Lebanon."

But the Europeans "are not going to deploy forces so long as we keep seeing conflict conditions on the ground," the ECFR's Barnes-Dacey pointed out. "If Europeans want to make a real difference at this stage, they could focus on pressuring Israel to pull back militarily while stepping up support to strengthen the Lebanese government."

Edited by: Andreas Illmer

entries.title: Bayreuth Festival: Ceremony and commemoration
entries.summary: To mark its 150th anniversary, the Bayreuth Festival remembers victims of the Holocaust — and confronts its founder's antisemitism.
entries.content:
July 29, 2026

To mark its 150th anniversary, the Bayreuth Festival remembers victims of the Holocaust — and confronts its founder's antisemitism.

"I would like to state explicitly that Katharina Wagner is changing the culture of remembrance in Bayreuth." With these words, spoken from the stage of the Bayreuth Festival, German-Jewish author Michel Friedman encapsulated the central message of the festival's two-day opening celebration.

Friedman spoke during a commemorative event titled "Silenced Voices," dedicated to Jewish artists who worked at the Bayreuth Festival and were later murdered or oppressed under the Nazi regime. Despite initial organizational turbulence, his talk became one of the key events of the opening celebrations on July 26, alongside the concert on the eve of the festival and the premiere of a new production of the opera "Rienzi."

Friedman also visited the exhibition with Bayreuth Festival director Katharina Wagner and several members of the local Jewish community. In the park surrounding the Bayreuth Festival grounds, directly beside the bust of Richard Wagner, a series of gray memorial steles stands as a powerful reminder of the Jewish artists whose lives were lost. A cantor from the Jewish community recited a prayer for the victims, and their names were read aloud.

'Democracy is in danger'

Friedman's speech in the Festspielhaus, which lasted more than an hour, encompassed far more than the omissions and blind spots of Germany's culture of remembrance. For the 70-year-old, whose family was almost entirely murdered during the Holocaust, the focus was on something more fundamental — the mechanisms that foster hatred and injustice, and the passivity of society that allows them to flourish. His message was about the present as much as the past.

Friedman criticized what he called a "bored, decadent democracy" and urged everyone present and everyone listening — as well as those outside the hall who remain "silent and grumbling”— to become active witnesses to their own time, before it is too late once again.

"My country, Germany, is a community. This community is defined by diversity, and diversity has once again become a concept that is under heavy attack. Yet this community and this diversity are the only future we have," he said.

A long history

Few places in Germany bring together history, culture and politics as strikingly as Bayreuth. The opening of this year's festival demonstrated that once again. To mark the festival's 150th anniversary, the red carpet was rolled out and graced by many of Germany's celebrities and politicians, including Chancellor Friedrich Merz, former Chancellor Angela Merkel as well as many international guests.

Inside the Festspielhaus, visitors were greeted by Bayreuth figures from the past century and a half, represented in a large mural by Hungarian street artist Adam Heat that dominates the auditorium.

At the center is King Ludwig II of Bavaria presenting Richard Wagner with a Grail overflowing with money — a vivid metaphor for the founding of the festival. Surrounding him is an illustrious cast of Bayreuth figures from the past 150 years — members of the Wagner family, who have guided the festival for generations; conductors ranging from Wilhelm Furtwängler and Arturo Toscanini to Oksana Lyniv and Nathalie Stutzmann. Also depicted is Wagner admirer and longtime Bayreuth guest Adolf Hitler, portrayed in elegant attire and holding a small glass.

Nike Wagner, the composer's great-granddaughter, summed up the message behind the work in her festival address: As visitors to the festival's grand hall, we become part of "Wagner's artistic ritual. Whoever takes a seat here now, sits with all those who have sat here before."

Katharina Wagner warns against the far-right

Katharina Wagner, Richard Wagner's descendant and the festival's artistic director spoke candidly about her family's Nazi ties. "Given my family's close and, in some cases, deeply personal ties to the Nazi regime, and given the role of the festival as a cultural showcase of the Third Reich, but also bearing in mind that our German democracy today is once again threatened by forces seeking to make antisemitism, racism, chauvinism, and nationalism part of the foundations of the state, there is no better place than this Festspielhaus to say: No."

In his speech, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz explained why, for him personally, Wagner's legacy and music represent the contradictions of German intellectual history:

"Richard Wagner's person and work are exemplary of both the greatness and the darker depths of Germany's artistic and historical legacy. They represent the uniquely German combination of the most admirable and the most questionable aspects of our past. When we engage with Wagner, we have the opportunity to see and hear so much of ourselves across the centuries in a single body of work."

And nowhere, Merz said, is this opportunity felt more profoundly than in Bayreuth.

With such direct statements during the anniversary event, the Bayreuth Festival has opened a new chapter in its culture of remembrance. In doing so, the festival seeks to make a broader social statement and take a firm stand against antisemitism.

This article was translated from German and edited by Teresa O'Connell.

entries.title: France: DJ Kavinsky found dead at Paris home
entries.summary: The star of the French electro scene, whose real name was Vincent Belorgey, was best known for his 2010 single Nightcall which he performed at the closing ceremony of the 2024 Olympic Games in Paris.
entries.content:
July 29, 2026

The star of the French electro scene, whose real name was Vincent Belorgey, was best known for his 2010 single Nightcall which he performed at the closing ceremony of the 2024 Olympic Games in Paris.

French DJ Vincent Belorgey, better known as DJ Kavinsky, was found dead at his home in Paris on Tuesday evening, French prosecutors confirmed on Wednesday.

"An inquiry into the cause of death has been opened to ​determine the circumstances of the death, as first responders found ⁠no suspicious ​elements at ​the scene," they said in a statement carried by the AFP news agency.

Belorgey was previously reported dead by Paris daily Le Parisien. He would have turned 51 years old on Friday, July 31.

The musician was best known for 2010 single Nightcall, which was featured in Nicolas Winding Refn's 2011 film Drive.  Belorgey also performed the single at the closing ceremony of the 2024 Olympic Games in Paris.

"With sudden loss of Kavinsky, France has lost one of her more unique voices," French Culture Minister Catherine Pegard said in a social media post.

"Simultaneously danceable and nostalgic, his music will continue to resonate across generations and borders."

Who was Kavinsky?

A self-taught pianist from Saint-Denis in the Paris region, Kavinsky launched his career in the early 2000s, notably serving as a supporting act for Daft Punk and performing alongside other emerging names in the electro scene, such as SebastiAn.

However, the major turning point in his career was "Nightcall"— a synth-wave hit with a dark atmosphere and a slowed-down tempo — which featured on the soundtrack of Drive, the Hollywood thriller starring Ryan Gosling.

"Kavinsky is a character I created because just putting my face on a record sleeve isn't something that suits me," Belorgey said in an interview back in 2007.

Belorgey described "Kavinsky" as someone who died in a car crash before returning as an undead DJ with blue skin and red eyes.

"Showing my own face holds absolutely no interest for me … When I'm making music, I have images in my head of films and television shows I liked when I was little. So I created this story that mixes all those memories together," Belorgey said.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

entries.title: Japan: Hospitals struggle after deadly Kumamoto earthquake
entries.summary: Rescuers are searching for survivors after a magnitude 7.1 earthquake struck southern Japan, killing over a dozen people and causing widespread damage. DW has more.
entries.content:
Japan

Japan: Hospitals struggle after deadly earthquake

Published July 29, 2026last updated July 29, 2026

Rescuers are searching for survivors after a magnitude 7.1 earthquake struck southern Japan, killing over a dozen people and causing widespread damage. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • A magnitude 7.1 earthquake struck southern Japan
  • At least 13 people have died
  • Rescuers are searching for missing employees at a partially collapsed mall
  • Five people were killed in a factory smokestack collapse
  • More than 36,000 homes are still without power.

Here is the latest on the aftermath of the earthquake in Japan:



Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section 'The strongest quake I have ever experienced'

'The strongest quake I have ever experienced'

Earthquake survivors have been describing the moment the 7.1 magnitude quake struck Japan's southwestern Kumamoto region.

"It was the strongest quake I have ever experienced," 73-year-old businessman Kanzo Matsuomoto told the AFP news agency. "I'm not sure if the region will recover from the damage."

Tokito Kitagawa was riding his motorcycle at the time of the earthquake and said: "Suddenly, there was a huge noise. I couldn't stay on my feet. I had to crouch down."

Kiyoshi Matsunaga, 74, was heading to the supermarket checkout just a few streets away from the collapsed Aeon shopping mall when the shaking began.

"I was frightened," he told the Associated Press, describing items being scattered from the supermarket shelves.

"I thought a bomb had gone off," Takateru Sonoda, 41, who runs a combined hair salon and café near the mall, told local news agency Jiji Press.

"There were people calling on others to evacuate and sirens were ringing out. Nearby roads were gridlocked, it ​was a state of panic."

Yuki Kiyozumi, deputy chief priest at a nearby temple, had just returned home from a meeting and was about to feed her cat. She recalled how she had to crawl on the floor because the shaking was so violent and said: "I don't even know if or how we can rebuild again."

Skip next section Hospitals struggle to cope near quake epicenter

Hospitals struggle to cope near quake epicenter

Hospitals near the epicenter have come under severe strain as power outages and a surge in casualties disrupt medical care.

A hospital in the Uki district said it was unable to operate after losing electricity in the earthquake.

"It's become like a field hospital," the head of its administrative department told Japanese public broadcaster NHK.

Another hospital in the city suspended new admissions after treating 86 injured people, including three in serious condition, saying it could no longer accept additional emergency cases.

Skip next section Rescuers scramble for survivors after Japan earthquake

Rescuers scramble for survivors after Japan earthquake

Rescuers are racing to find survivors after a magnitude 7.1 earthquake struck southern Japan, killing at least 13 people and leaving widespread damage across the region.

Eight people were pulled from the rubble of a partially collapsed shopping mall near the city of Kumamoto after an apparent explosion around an hour after Tuesday's quake. However, three of those rescued later died.

Mall operator Aeon said four employees remained unaccounted for after checks on around 2,700 staff members. Customers had been evacuated immediately after the initial earthquake.

"Even now, there are people waiting to be rescued, and this is a race against time. We will marshal all available resources on the ground to save and rescue as many people as possible," Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said from Tokyo.

Authorities are investigating whether a gas explosion caused the collapse at the Aeon mall. While rescuers reported smelling gas inside the building, government spokesperson Minoru Kihara said the cause was still unclear.

Firefighters, police and around 170 military personnel concentrated their efforts on sections of the mall where calls for help had been heard.

More than 4,500 soldiers have been deployed across the disaster zone as emergency crews search damaged buildings, restore power and assess ruptured roads.

Skip next section Five killed in factory chimney collapse

Five killed in factory chimney collapse

In the city of Yatsushiro, five people were killed when part of a red-and-white smokestack collapsed at a Nippon Paper Industries factory, according to the Kumamoto prefectural government's disaster response team.

Seven people were rescued from the debris, but four others were still believed to be trapped.

Skip next section Widespread infrastructure damage

Widespread infrastructure damage

About 260,000 people across Kumamoto prefecture have been told to seek shelter as damaged buildings, buckled roads and a collapsed bridge reveal the scale of the destruction.

Police received hundreds of emergency calls after the earthquake, including reports of collapsed structures and people in need of rescue.

The epicentre was around 20 kilometers (12.5 miles) south of Kumamoto City, the largest city in the central part of Kyushu island and home to about 700,000 people. Over 100 aftershocks followed the initial quake.

The port city of Yatsushiro was among the worst-hit areas. Part of a local bridge fell into the Kumagawa River, while authorities warned residents to remain alert for further powerful tremors and landslides over the coming week.

The earthquake reached the maximum level of 7 on Japan's seismic intensity scale in some areas.

More than 36,000 homes remained without electricity on Wednesday as temperatures climbed to around 34 degrees Celsius, prompting authorities to issue heatstroke warnings.

Skip next section Major manufacturers halt production

Major manufacturers halt production

Several major companies, including Renesas Electronics, Sony, Tokyo Electron and Honda, have suspended operations in their Kumamoto plants following the earthquake.

Toyota Motor said it would also halt work at three factories outside Kumamoto prefecture through Friday because of the impact on suppliers.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, the world's largest contract chipmaker, evacuated employees from its local plant as a precaution after the quake.

The company said it began gradually resuming operations late on Tuesday.

Skip next section How prone is the region to earthquakes?

How prone is the region to earthquakes?

Japan is one of the world's most earthquake-prone countries because it lies on the Pacific "Ring of Fire," a belt of volcanoes and ocean trenches where several tectonic plates meet.

The country accounts for around 20% of the world's earthquakes of magnitude 6.0 or higher.

The Kumamoto prefecture was struck by a devastating earthquake 10 years ago that killed 275 people, injured another 2,739 and damaged thousands of buildings.

The walls of Kumamoto Castle, one of the city's main tourist attractions, were badly damaged in that disaster.

The castle was damaged once again in Tuesday's earthquake. The tremblor also affected local shrines and a 17th-century tea house.

entries.title: Germany: How effective are exit programs for Islamists?
entries.summary: Germany has set up many programs to help individuals break away from the radical Islamist scene. Following the Islamist terror attack on Berlin's Pride event, critics say the programs are ineffective.
entries.content:
July 29, 2026

Germany has set up many programs to help individuals break away from the radical Islamist scene. Following the Islamist terror attack on Berlin's Pride event, critics say the programs are ineffective.

Following Saturday's deadly attack by suspected Islamist assailant Abdul B. against Berlin's Pride event, a debate has erupted in Germany over what lessons the country should draw from the incident. The 21-year-old, who was later shot and killed by police while he was on the run, had had two intake interviews in June and July as part of a deradicalization program in Berlin.

However, according to Thomas Mücke, executive director of the Violence Prevention Network, it did not appear that Abdul B. genuinely wanted to turn his back on the Islamist scene — and it is unlikely that he would have been accepted into the program.

Similar cases have also occurred periodically in the Islamism Exit Program (API). 

"We then have to conclude that assistance in exiting is not possible at that point because we have no reason to believe the individual actually wants to distance themselves." API exit program counselor and social worker Stefanie Adler* tells DW.



The Islamism Exit Program API is based in Germany's most populous state of North Rhine-Westphalia, was established in 2014 to support people who want to break away from Islamist circles, including many who are considered potential threats by security services.

"What we've seen over the past two years is that we're dealing with younger and younger individuals. In the past, we saw people traveling to Syria, and it was more or less clear that they went there and joined the Islamic State, became radicalized in the real world," Adler explains.

Today, she says, they are younger, and they are often radicalized through digital media. "Social media acts as an amplifier for radicalization — and it happens much faster," Adler adds.

Deradicalization is a 'long and arduous process'

Some individuals do not approach the API on their own initiative, while other potential candidates are reported to the police or youth court services by contact persons in correctional facilities.

"We then take a closer look at the person," said API deradicalization counselor and psychologist Viola Geiger*, "gather information, and begin the counseling process — initially on a weekly basis, and toward the end, sometimes every few months. It's definitely a lengthy process."

Once an individual has credibly distanced themself from violence as a legitimate course of action and learned to cope with crisis situations on their own, they are considered successfully deradicalized and their cases are closed. But achieving this requires patience and persistence.

In one case, API exit program counselors worked with one individual for as long as seven years. In spite of these challenges, says Stefanie Adler, deradicalization programs are absolutely essential.

"What would be the alternative if these programs didn't exist? Many people who are released from prison after serving a sentence need such programs to reintegrate into society," said Adler. And the public is largely unaware of the many success stories. "People forget that those who have successfully left the movement then fly under the radar and no longer appear in public because they simply want to live their lives."

The effect of global political instability

Forty organizations and initiatives working on prevention, disengagement or deradicalization in the area of religiously motivated extremism are organized under the umbrella association the Federal Working Group on Religiously Motivated Extremism, or BAG RelEx for short. Its executive director, Jamuna Oehlmann, was just as shocked as many others after the attack in Berlin.

However, she told DW that the problem of radical Islamism in Germany remains significant.

"There are also more and more young women who are becoming radicalized. But still, it is above all young men in Germany who are becoming radicalized, who commit acts of violence and who act out their violent fantasies," Oehlmann says.

Radicalization is a process with many contributing factors, she explains, where various elements converge and, in the worst-case scenario, lead to radicalization. "Society and external factors play an important role in this, but so does the responsibility of each individual who becomes radicalized."

Oehlmann identified specific crisis situations, or "push factors," that can cause people to become alienated from society. These include the loss of a beloved parent, failing an exam, a housing crisis, job loss, experiences of discrimination, exclusion and bullying. Additionally, the global increase in political instability is also driving people to despair.

"Then there are Islamist groups who know how to take advantage of these life crises and target young people by giving them the feeling: 'You will be heard with us, you belong with us, you can be someone with us.' And in addition, they simplify the complexity of the world by breaking it down into good and evil, black and white."

Deradicalization programs threatened by budget cuts

That's why it's all the more important that funding for organizations working to prevent or deradicalize Islamists not be cut. However, Federal Minister of Education Karin Prien has announced exactly that.

Minister Prien plans to restructure the Live Democracy! funding program. Funding for approximately 200 projects is set to expire at the end of the year. Twenty-three of the 40 member organizations of the Federal Working Group on Religiously Motivated Extremism are affected by this.

Jamuna Oehlmann is critical of this decision. "The problem is that even projects that are doing good work are affected by this. And so now they're having to focus on fundraising — that is, finding new sources of funding — instead of concentrating on the actual work of preventing Islamism. We need reliability and a long-term approach."

*Name has been changed to protect privacy

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Germany news: BMW to cut up to 8,000 jobs
entries.summary: The auto giant BMW has become the latest German car company to announce major job cuts, projected to shed 8,000 by the end of 2027. Meanwhile, new ministers have been appointed to the German government. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: BMW to cut up to 8,000 jobs

Published July 29, 2026last updated July 29, 2026

The auto giant BMW has become the latest German car company to announce major job cuts, projected to shed 8,000 by the end of 2027. Meanwhile, new ministers have been appointed to the German government. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • The German automaker BMW intends to cut 8,000 office jobs
  • The German government's cabinet reshuffle has been formalized
  • Veteran goalkeeper Manuel Neuer says he will 'very likely' retire after the coming football season

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Thorsten Frei confirmed as conservative parliamentary faction chief

Thorsten Frei confirmed as conservative parliamentary faction chief

Thorsten Frei was confirmed as the parliamentary faction chief of the conservative bloc on Wednesday afternoon.

In a vote at a special session of lawmakers from the governing CDU and CSU parties, Frei received 91.9% of the vote.

Frei, a close confidant of Friedrich Merz, previously served as the chancellor's chief of staff. He replaces Jens Spahn, who stepped down as faction chief this month after it became known that he and his partner had a child via surrogacy, a practice that is prohibited in Germany and which Spahn himself had spoken out against in the past.

Skip next section German Cabinet backs AI-assisted processing of asylum applications

German Cabinet backs AI-assisted processing of asylum applications

Germany's Cabinet, led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz, approved legislation on Wednesday that would allowartificial intelligence to assist authorities in processing asylum, visa and residence permit applications.

The proposed law aims to "speed up administrative processes, enable more targeted use of resources, and facilitate a systematic evaluation of current practices."

In recent years, government agencies responsible for migration issues have faced consistently high application numbers, while staff remains limited. As a result, applicants often experience long waiting periods for decisions.

The bill aims to provide a legal framework for how government agencies can use AI to support data analysis and decision-making.

It also allows migration officials to use application data to train and test AI models. Administrators would also be permitted to analyze data from previous cases to identify patterns in decision-making, which could lead to harmonized and accelerated workflows.

The government stressed, however, that AI would only be a supporting tool for officials and that final assessments and rulings in each case would remain the responsibility of human caseworkers.

Skip next section Goalkeeper Manuel Neuer says retirement 'very likely'

Goalkeeper Manuel Neuer says retirement 'very likely'

Bayern Munich goalkeeper Manuel Neuer said he was "very likely" to go into retirement the end of the upcoming season.

Neuer, who is 40 years old and also captain of the Bayern team, has had an accomplished career, winning 13 Bundesliga and two Champions League titles with the team.

Moreover, as goalie of the German national team, he was part of the winning squad in the 2014 World Cup in Brazil.

Neuer retired from international football after the European Championship 2024 only to temporarily come out of retirement for the 2026 World Cup, a decision that did not come without controversy.

Speaking to reporters during the training camp in Southern Bavaria, he expressed hope that the upcoming Bayern season would help overcome the frustration of Germany's poor showing at the World Cup, which ended in a Round of 32 loss to Paraguay.

Neuer also credited the Bayern team and structure for staying on.

"In perhaps 85% of cases, I would have stopped," Neuer said.

"But with this team, the staff and the coaching team, it is simply a lot of fun. We always have the chance to compete for every title and this squad is right at the highest level."

Skip next section Germany reshuffles Cabinet after Spahn resignation

Germany reshuffles Cabinet after Spahn resignation

Germany's government has moved forward with a Cabinet reshuffle sparked by the resignation of conservative parliamentary group leader Jens Spahn.

President Frank-Walter Steinmeier formally appointed Nina Warken as head of the Federal Chancellery on Wednesday, along with Carsten Linnemann as health minister and Steffen Bilger as transport minister.

The three politicians received their certificates of appointment at a ceremony in Berlin.

Thorsten Frei, whom Warken replaces at the Chancellery, is due to be elected later on Wednesday as leader of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative parliamentary bloc.

The reshuffle comes as Merz's government struggles in opinion polls ahead of three closely watched state elections in September, where the far-right Alternative for Germany is expected to make significant gains.

Skip next section Carmaking giant BMW to cut up to 8,000 jobs

Carmaking giant BMW to cut up to 8,000 jobs

BMW aims to cut up to 8,000 by the end of 2027, according to company sources. The German carmaker said the reduction would primarily target office jobs, while production line workers will be spared from cuts. 

The Munich-based automaker hopes to achieve the cuts through natural staff turnover as well as a voluntary redundancy scheme. The latter would be aimed at all employees in Germany not directly involved in production, who could choose to accept severance packages in a period from October 2026 to the end of 2027.

The company currently employs 84,000 staff in Germany, and roughly 154,000 globally.

BMW is the latest German car company to announce job cuts, following similar moves by rival brands Volkswagen, Mercedes and Volkswagen-owned Audi. 

Germany  prestigious car industry is struggling amid stiff competition from Chinese carmakers, US tariffs, and narrower profit margins from electric cars.

BMW was long considered one of the sector's more resilient players. The planned cuts come after the company warned last month that its sales in China were falling sharply.

Skip next section Lawmakers expected to endorse Merz's picks for new government ministers

Lawmakers expected to endorse Merz's picks for new government ministers

After conservative parliamentary group leader Jens Spahn quit over a surrogacy scandal. Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced a series of top-level changes in the German government.

On Wednesday, members of the conservative bloc are meeting in a special session where they are expected to approve Merz's picks, including the choice of Thorsten Frei as a replacement to Spahn as the conservatives new parliamentary faction chief.

Later in the day, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier will appoint a series of new ministers. Nina Warken is to take over as the chancellery's new chief of staff, while Carsten Linneman is to become health minister, and Steffen Bilger to take over as transport minister.

Merz has faced significant backlash in his own party for replacing Transport Minister Patrick Schnieder, who hails from Rhineland Palatinate, as other conservatives from the western German state protested the move.

Under Germany's constitution, incoming ministers are required to take an official oath before parliament, the Bundestag. However, with the Bundestag currently in its summer recess, the swearing-in is expected to take place only when lawmakers return in September 9.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage!

Welcome to our coverage!

Temperatures are rising in Bonn once again as DW's online news team wishes you a Guten Tag  and welcomes you to our latest  Germany news blog.

BMW has said it intends to cut 8,000 jobs, as it joins a growing list of major German carmakers undertaking significant workforce reductions.

Meanwhile, President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is expected to appoint the new government ministers after the ruling coalition lawmakers confirm the candidates picked by Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Follow us for these and other stories from Germany.

entries.title: India news: Police issue FIRs over 'abusive' posts against Modi
entries.summary: Delhi police asked X to provide details on users who allegedly posted or shared "abusive" content on Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Follow DW for more.
entries.content:
Asia

India news: Police issue FIRs over 'abusive' posts on Modi

Published July 29, 2026last updated July 29, 2026

Delhi police asked X to provide details on users who allegedly posted or shared "abusive" content on Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Follow DW for more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Delhi Police files First Incident Reports over alleged anti-Modi posts
  • Social media platform X asked to remove targeted content, provide info on users
  • Death toll in Assam floods rises to 75

Read below a roundup of the biggest headlines from India on Wednesday, July 29:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Assam floods death toll rises to 75

Assam floods death toll rises to 75

The death toll in the Assam flood has risen to 75, with seven more deaths reported in the last 24 hours, even though the number of affected people has decreased to 332,000, officials said on Wednesday.

The state government has increased the ex gratia amount to the families of the deceased from 400,000 Indian rupees (€3,675, $4,180) to 900,000 Indian rupees and relaxed the norms for availing the compensation, officials said, according to a PTI report.

The flood-hit population was 332,000. Charaideo was the worst-hit district, affecting 142,000 people, followed by Sivasagar (97,074) and Jorhat (57,371).

Skip next section Anti-paper leak bill with raised penalties passed in Lok Sabha

Anti-paper leak bill with raised penalties passed in Lok Sabha

India's lower house of parliament, the Lok Sabha, on Wednesday passed a bill to amend the anti-paper leak law, introducing stricter punishment of up to 10 years' imprisonment and a fine of Rs 50 lakh (~€46,000).

The Public Examination (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill was introduced in the house by Union Minister Jitendra Singh, days after mass protests rocked the capital.

Speaking in the Lok Sabha, Singh said the government had acted swiftly in the NEET paper leak case and that 52 FIRs had been registered since the anti-paper leak law came into force in 2024.

The bill was passed after heated debate. During the discussion, Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi alleged that Home Minister Amit Shah had authorized police excesses against student protesters.

Skip next section India condemns attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz at UNSC

India condemns attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz at UNSC

India strongly condemned the recent attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. 

Addressing a UN Security Council during an open debate on the Middle East, India's Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Parvathaneni Harish, said the resurgence of hostilities after a brief lull was "worrying." He called for a return to dialogue and diplomacy.

India also urged for restoration of unimpeded navigation and trade through international waterways in the region.

Harish said the Middle East region is of "immense importance" to India. 

The UN ambassador noted that the violence directly affected Indians, following the news that merchant vessels, including GFS Galaxy, MT Al Bahiyah and MT Mombasa were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz.

“Several Indian citizens were injured, including some seriously, one Indian tragically lost his life, and one is missing, in these attacks," he said.

Skip next section Supreme Court orders release of minors arrested during CJP protest

Supreme Court orders release of minors arrested during CJP protest

India's Supreme Court has issued orders for the release of minors arrested during the CJP protests.

It said authorities must ensure surveillance footage is preserved after petitioners alleged police brutality against demonstrators.

Chief Justice Surya Kant also told authorities to preserve the digital and personal data of people who joined the protests, while also barring any coercive action against ​them, according to the Indian media.

The court also told authorities to ensure protesters' data was not made public.

Reportedly, the Supreme Court's intervention came after petitions were filed by student protesters and activists. The protesters seek ​action against police for allegedly using excessive force and pellet guns during the CJP rallies.

"Whoever has committed excess ... atrocities on innocent people, the law will take care of them. For that, there needs to be a completely independent and fair investigation," Kant said, according to legal website Live Law, one of several outlets reporting the ruling.

"A probe is meaningless if ​no responsibility is fixed," he said, before ordering the interim steps.

Skip next section Delhi Police issues notice over abusive posts against Modi

Delhi Police issues notice over abusive posts against Modi

The Delhi Police has continued its crackdown against CJP protesters with it now filing a First Information Report (FIR) against several social media accounts which allegedly posted abusive content against Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

The Delhi Police has asked X to delete and remove the alleged post or video from the platform immediately.

Police have also issued a notice to X, seeking details on users who allegedly posted or shared the content under investigation.

Delhi Police's Social Media Monitoring Team has been tracking content across platforms to identify posts that allegedly violate existing laws or have the potential for public disorder, officials said.

A case has been registered by the Intelligence Fusion and Strategic Operations (IFSO) unit of the Special Cell under charges of criminal intimidation, public mischief and defamation, Indian newspaper The New Indian Express reported.

It is not clear how many accounts have been served the notices.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! This is Midhat from the New Delhi bureau bringing you the latest news from India.

The crackdown on dissenters in the aftermath of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) is continuing with the Delhi police issuing notices to accounts on X over abusive posts against Indian PM Narendra Modi.

Meanwhile, the Supreme Court of India has directed authorities to release minors arrested during the CJP protests.

Stay tuned for all this and more from India!

entries.title: US bans Chinese and foreign-made humanoid robots
entries.summary: The Trump administration has banned the import of humanoid and quadruped robots manufactured outside the United States, citing national security concerns. The ban could strain diplomatic tensions with China.
entries.content:
July 29, 2026

The Trump administration has banned the import of humanoid and quadruped robots manufactured outside the United States, citing national security concerns. The ban could strain diplomatic tensions with China.

The United States has announced a ban on the import of foreign-made humanoid and quadruped robots in a move which will likely exclude Chinese manufacturers from the US market and could strain tensions between Washington and Beijing.

The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Tuesday that "advanced robotic devices" produced abroad posed national and cyber security risks to the United States.

The decision was based on findings from a White House task force which concluded that foreign-built robots could create "a cybersecurity risk that threatens the security of critical infrastructure" and "the safety and security" of US residents.

The FCC defines the relevant mobile robots as devices weighing more than two kilograms that use sensors, network connectivity and software to achieve autonomous navigation, including the avoidance of obstacles.

China dominates the market in humanoid robots

The market for humanoid and quadruped (also known as four-legged "robot dogs") is seen as a major international growth area, with US and Chinese companies competing to develop the technology.

And China has a clear lead, with analysts at Barclays estimating that Chinese-made humanoid robots account for around 85% of the global market share. Morgan Stanley experts predict that China's humanoid robot market could be worth $15 billion (€13.2 billion) by 2030.

"Chinese manufacturers have been scaling production and reducing costs faster than most overseas competitors," Morningstar analyst Kangyuxiao Li told the Associated Press.

In the US, firms such as Figure AI are already deploying humanoid robots on production lines, while tech giant Tesla plans to begin production of its "Optimus" robot this year.

Currently, however, US robot exports remain in their hundreds while Unitree and AGIBOT, two of China's biggest advanced robotics companies, each shipped more than 5,000 humanoid robots in 2025 alone, according to the technology research and advisory group Omdia.

FCC chairman Brendan Carr said the ban was also aimed at "secur[ing] America's critical supply chains."

But Li said the measures would not "materially slow China's overall humanoid development, given the size of its domestic manufacturing base and opportunities in other export markets."

Trump-Xi summit: the diplomatic ramifications

Beyond the industrial market effects, the FCC ban could also have diplomatic consequences ahead of a meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese Premier Xi Jinping in September.

The US has already banned imports of Chinese-made drones and is considering restrictions on Chinese open-source artificial intelligence (AI) models, citing cybersecurity concerns including espionage, surveillance and data collection.

The Pentagon recently placed Unitree and several other major Chinese technology companies on its list of firms which it claims have links to the Chinese military, a claim that Beijing said it "firmly opposes."

"It's a steady drumbeat of potential flashpoints heading into [the] Trump-Xi summit," said Samm Sacks, a senior fellow at New America, a think tank focused on Chinese technology policies.

Most humanoid robots are currently used for industrial applications in confined spaces, such as automobile factories or storage warehouses. Stationary industrial robots are to be exempt from the FCC ban but the definition could also cover advanced robot vacuum cleaners.

The FCC also added foreign-made power inverters to the list – devices that, among other functions, convert direct current from solar panels into standard alternating current, which can be used by the electrical grid.

The agency cited similar cybersecurity concerns, saying network-connected inverters could be remotely disabled or used to collect data.

Like the ban on humanoid robots, the restrictions on inverters are also expected to hit Chinese manufacturers hardest, given that they currently dominate the global solar inverter market.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher
